archetype.name: Game Manager (short-area, run-supported)
archetype.definition: A quarterback who works mostly underneath, behind a top-tier running game, and lives on timing throws to the middle of the field. This year he has given back almost everything that requires pushing the ball past 10 yards.

report.headline: Last year's breakout is gone downfield; what's left is a short-game survivor.
report.take:
Daniel Jones arrived in Indianapolis last year and posted the best season of his career. He averaged 8.08 yards per attempt, a +2.3 CPOE and 0.193 EPA per play, a level he had only approached once before, in 2022. Six games into 2026, almost all of that is gone. He sits at -0.121 EPA per dropback (35th of 45), 5.92 yards per attempt and a -3.23 CPOE, all well below the league average. The career line explains why that matters: outside 2022 and 2025, his EPA per play has hovered around zero or below, and 2023 looked a lot like this. The fair read is that last season was his ceiling, not his new baseline, and he has fallen back past his norm.

The decline sits in one place: depth. Under 10 air yards he is still a functional quarterback. He completes 71.9% with a positive CPOE and +0.161 EPA on 0-9 yard throws, and all four of his touchdowns came in that range. At 10-plus air yards he completes 35.2% with a -12.7 CPOE, four interceptions and no touchdowns. On throws of 20-plus yards it gets worse: 4 of 28 by completion rate, a -23.1 CPOE and -0.436 EPA a throw. His bad-throw rate (11.5%) is essentially last year's, and his aggressiveness has dropped 3.5 points. Both suggest this is less about wild accuracy than about nothing open, and nothing landing, downfield. Alec Pierce has been limited to two games and is now on IR, and the timing fits, though the dossier can't prove the link.

Two other things drag the line down. The first is ball security: six interceptions and three lost fumbles (42nd of 45) for a passer who isn't creating many big plays to offset them. The second is sacks. His protection is good on paper (pressured on 15% of dropbacks, sixth-lowest), yet he still takes 2.5 sacks a game. Week 6 against Tennessee was the worst of it: six sacks with a 3.12-second time to throw, holding the ball when nothing came open deep. He isn't the scrambler he was with the Giants either. He has seven scrambles all year, and his rushing is down to 9.2 yards a game. His few designed runs, mostly short-yardage and goal-line looks, have been efficient.

The Colts' offense now runs through Jonathan Taylor's ground game, which ranks second in rush EPA, while the pass offense ranks 28th. Jones is being asked to keep the chains moving underneath, and he can do that. What he can't do right now is win when the defense takes the short game away, and the last three games trend the wrong way: 54.2% completions and a -5.8 CPOE.

strengths.title: Short and middle timing throws
strengths.body: Throws under 10 air yards are a positive-EPA, high-completion part of his game, and all four touchdowns came there. The middle of the field is his best direction at +0.241 EPA a throw, which fits the Downs-and-Warren option routes this offense leans on. This has held across his career and is the part of the profile you can count on.

strengths.title: Clean pockets, low pressure rate
strengths.body: He is pressured on just 15% of dropbacks, sixth-lowest among qualifiers, so the line and the quick-game structure are generally holding up. That should keep his floor from collapsing against ordinary pass rushes.

strengths.title: Designed runs in tight spaces
strengths.body: His eight designed runs have a 0.875 success rate and +0.849 EPA a play, with a touchdown. They gain few yards but convert short downs. The usage is limited, but it is a real red-zone and short-yardage tool, not luck.

concerns.title: The deep ball has disappeared
concerns.body: He has 4 completions on 28 throws of 20-plus yards with a -23.1 CPOE and no touchdowns. The whole 10-plus range runs at -0.105 EPA with four picks. His bad-throw rate hasn't changed from last year, which points to a missing vertical target (Pierce on IR) and coverage dictating terms more than a broken arm. Still, last year's 8.08 YPA has fallen to 5.92, and that won't return until someone wins downfield.

concerns.title: Turnovers without the payoff
concerns.body: Six interceptions plus three lost fumbles, with four turnover-worthy fumbles, is a lot of giveaway for an offense averaging 0.67 passing TDs a game. Interceptions have been a career-long trait, ranking poorly most seasons, so this is partly who he is. The fumble count should cool, but it won't vanish.

concerns.title: Sacks on non-pressured holds
concerns.body: A low pressure rate should produce a low sack rate, yet he takes 2.5 sacks a game, and Week 6 brought six of them with his longest time to throw of the season. When nothing is open deep he holds the ball rather than taking the checkdown, and that habit will hurt most against a strong pass rush.

trend.note: Week 2 at Kansas City (+5.9 EPA) is the only clearly positive game. The last three have slipped further: a 54.2% completion rate and -5.8 CPOE, with longer air yards in Weeks 5-6 producing yardage but not efficiency.

nextGame.headline: The league's best defense meets a passer with no deep answer
nextGame.body:
Minnesota ranks first in defensive EPA, pass EPA, rush EPA, success rate, hit rate and sack rate, and allows the fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks (8.4 a game). That is the worst possible draw for this version of Jones. The Vikings are sixth against short passes, which squeezes the one area where he has been efficient, and their 0.095 sack rate attacks the habit of holding the ball that produced six sacks last week. Offenses also run much more often than usual against them, and Indianapolis's second-ranked rushing attack makes that the likely plan. That keeps his volume modest and puts the game on Jonathan Taylor.

Availability hurts him on both counts. Tyler Warren, a 91%-snap tight end and his second-most productive target by EPA, is listed out. Pierce remains on IR with no practice window opening this week, Ashton Dulin is out and Anthony Gould is in the concussion protocol. That leaves Josh Downs, Keenan Allen and a thin cast, and Minnesota has held WR3s and tight ends below their averages. On the other side, Minnesota's offense is weak (last in success rate) and has questionable tags on Addison, Darrisaw and Hockenson. That points to a low-scoring, grind-it-out game consistent with the 41.5 total, not a shootout that inflates his passing numbers.

keyMatchups.title: Vikings pass rush vs. late holds
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota leads the league in hit rate and sack rate. Jones has taken sacks even behind clean pockets, so if the ball doesn't come out on time, this could be a repeat of Week 6.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs. stingy underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: His positive EPA lives under 10 air yards, and Minnesota ranks sixth in short-pass EPA allowed. Without Warren over the middle, Downs (+0.291 EPA a target) has to carry the quick game nearly alone.

keyMatchups.title: Low-total, run-heavy game script
keyMatchups.body: Offenses lean on the run against Minnesota, the Colts' rushing attack is a strength, and the Vikings' offense rarely sustains drives. Expect fewer dropbacks and a game decided by field position and turnovers.

nextGame.watch: Whether he gets the ball out on time on early downs, or holds it and takes sacks again the way he did against Tennessee.

restOfSeason.body:
The short game, the low pressure rate and a strong run game behind him are sustainable, so the floor is a passer who moves the chains in the 200-yard range. The deep-ball collapse is the swing piece. Some of it should regress toward his career norm once Pierce returns (estimated early November) and Warren is back, because 4-of-28 deep is extreme even for him, and his bad-throw rate hasn't changed from his best season. The lost fumbles should also slow. Don't expect last year's 8-plus YPA back. His career says 2025 was the outlier, and in this offense the job is managing games behind Taylor.

Expect roughly 195 to 235 passing yards a game, touchdowns rising a little from his 1.8% TD rate with healthier targets, and interceptions staying a problem. The passing-TD rate is the one most likely to improve. The turnover rate is the one least likely to.
swingFactors: Pierce's return restoring a vertical threat
Warren's groin and how many games he misses
Whether he cuts the sacks on clean-pocket holds

confidence.note: Six games and a 28-attempt deep sample, but a long career gives a clear baseline.
